findings.title: chemtrails 'past' trail shows ~the whole trajectory for the first tail_duration seconds, then snaps to empty (matplotlib 2D+3D)
findings.description: In update_lines_parallel (hypertools/plot/matplotlib_backend.py:992-993) and update_lines_parallel_2d (:1697-1698) the past trail is set with `data[0 : num - tail_duration + 1]` where `tail_duration` is window_frames (frame_rate * tail_duration seconds, 60 at gallery defaults). For num < window_frames - 1 the slice stop is NEGATIVE, so Python wraps it: the 'past' trail renders the FIRST n - window + num + 1 points. On the verbatim chemtrails.py example (901 frames, window 60) frame 0 draws 842/901 points (93% of the trajectory, most of it FUTURE data) as the faded 'past' trail, growing to 900 points at frame 58, snapping to 0 at frame 59, then regrowing correctly. Every matplotlib chemtrails animation therefore opens with a full-trajectory 'spoiler' that abruptly vanishes ~2s in. Also degrades animate_trails_mix.py: at frame 0 all three per-dataset styles look identical (all full trails), defeating the example's point. The plotly backend clamps its equivalent slice (plotly_backend.py:2142 `arr[:start + 1]`) and behaves correctly, so the two backends visibly diverge for identical inputs, contradicting the mirror-the-matplotlib-renderer parity notes. Fix: clamp the stop, e.g. `data[0 : max(0, num - tail_duration + 1)]` in both functions.
findings.repro:
import matplotlib; matplotlib.use('Agg')
import hypertools as hyp
data = hyp.load('weights_avg')
fig, ani = hyp.plot(data, animate=True, chemtrails=True)
seq = list(ani.new_frame_seq()); ani._init_draw()
trails = [ln for ln in fig.axes[0].get_lines() if abs((ln.get_alpha() or 1) - 0.3) < 1e-6]
for i in [0, 30, 58, 59, 60, 120]:
    ani._draw_frame(seq[i])
    print(i, [len(t.get_data_3d()[0]) for t in trails])
findings.expected: Past trail empty (0 points) at frame 0, growing smoothly as frames advance (as the plotly backend does: 2/7/17/31 points at frames 0/5/15/29 with duration=2, frame_rate=15).

findings.title: animate_plotly.py cannot finish in reasonable time: 900-frame kaleido gif export killed at 420s (estimated 15-25 min)
findings.description: The example's second call (`hyp.plot(data, animate='spin', duration=30, backend='plotly', save_path='spin.gif', show=False)`) exports via _export_animation_file (hypertools/plot/plotly_backend.py:1046), which renders EVERY one of the 900 frames to PNG through kaleido/Chromium one snapshot at a time. Run verbatim it was still running at 420s and was hard-killed with no spin.gif produced. A sanctioned 5-frame probe (duration=1, frame_rate=5) completed in 14.4s including ~5s kaleido startup, i.e. ~1.5-2s/frame, extrapolating to ~15-25 minutes for the verbatim 900 frames -- two orders of magnitude slower than the matplotlib exporter (save_movie.py wrote a 901-frame mp4 in 7.3s total). Any docs build or user copy-paste of this example stalls for tens of minutes with no progress feedback. Partly infra-flavored: kaleido subprocesses are also known to wedge entirely (pyproject.toml cites a 6h hang on Windows CI), so the export may never finish at all on some machines. Suggested fixes: drastically reduce the exported animation in the example (e.g. duration=3, frame_rate=10 => 30 frames ~= 1 min), and/or batch frames through a persistent kaleido session, and/or emit a progress/cost warning in _export_animation_file for large frame counts.

findings.title: animate_plotly.py writes spin.gif into the CWD and the 6.8MB generated artifact is committed to the repo
findings.description: animate_plotly.py uses a bare relative `save_path='spin.gif'`, unlike save_image.py and save_movie.py which both write into `tempfile.mkdtemp()`. sphinx-gallery executes examples with the example dir as CWD, so building the docs (or a user running the script) drops a multi-MB gif wherever they happen to be -- and indeed `examples/spin.gif` (6,792,550 bytes, git-tracked, dated Jul 6 15:52) is a committed build artifact of this example, bloating the repo and guaranteeing a dirty tree on every docs rebuild. Fix: use the same tempfile pattern as the other save examples, and remove examples/spin.gif from version control (docs thumbnails live under docs/_static/thumbnails).

findings.title: Docstring parity claim 'Both backends generate exactly frame_rate * duration frames' is off by one for matplotlib animate=True/'parallel'/'window'
findings.description: hypertools/plot/plot.py's frame_rate docstring states 'Both backends generate exactly frame_rate * duration frames, so matplotlib and plotly animations play at identical speed, duration, and framerate.' Measured: matplotlib animate=True produces duration*frame_rate + 1 frames (901 at defaults; 61 at duration=2; 31 at duration=2/frame_rate=15 -- the FuncAnimation frame count is the interpolated data length x[0].shape[0], matplotlib_backend.py:1605-1608), while plotly produces exactly duration*frame_rate (900/30 measured) and matplotlib spin/serial also produce exactly 900/60. The exported save_movie mp4 accordingly has nb_frames=901, duration 30.033s. Harmless in practice but the documented 'exactly'/'identical' parity is false for the most common animate mode; either trim the interpolated array by one or soften the claim.

findings.title: animate_surface_morph.py per-frame timing claim ('roughly 20ms/frame instead of ~100ms+') does not reproduce (measured 91ms vs 370ms)
findings.description: The example docstring claims the smoothing=2 cap gives 'roughly 20ms/frame instead of ~100ms+ (measured on this machine)' vs the library-default 3 rounds. Measured on this machine (Apple silicon, Agg, timing ani._draw_frame + canvas.draw over 20 consecutive frames, no savefig): smoothing=2 hold = 91ms/frame, transition = 81ms/frame; smoothing=3 hold = 370ms/frame. The direction and the ~4x ratio are right, but both absolute numbers are ~4x higher than documented, so the '20ms' figure is not reproducible as written (it may describe only the smooth_hull_3d step rather than the per-frame cost the sentence implies). The example's other numeric claims all verified exactly: 360 total frames, morph_schedule [60,15,60,15,60,15,60,15,60].

findings.title: Exported GIFs play ~10% faster than the requested duration at the default frame_rate=30 (33.33ms rounds to 30ms centiseconds)
findings.description: GIF frame delays are stored in centiseconds. Both exporters request 1000/frame_rate ms per frame (PillowWriter fps in hypertools/plot/animate.py:32; frame_ms in plotly_backend.py:1116), so at the default frame_rate=30 the 33.33ms delay is stored as 30ms and a '30-second' animation plays in 27.0s (measured: hyper_animation docstring example trajectory.gif, 900 frames, playback 27.0s; small gif at frame_rate=15: 66.7 -> 60ms, 0.96s for a 1s animation). The animate.py comment block (lines 22-27) promises 'an exported file plays in real time ... total ~= duration seconds'. Consider snapping exported-gif delays to a centisecond-representable rate (e.g. distribute 33/34ms alternately, or document the quantization). MP4 export is exact (30.033s for 901 frames).

findings.title: save_path failure modes are cryptic: unsupported extension yields a raw ffmpeg CalledProcessError after rendering all frames; nonexistent directory a bare FileNotFoundError
findings.description: In stark contrast to the excellent animate-kwarg validation errors, save_path is never validated up front. (a) `save_path='anim.xyz'` falls through _save_animation's else-branch to the ffmpeg writer, renders every frame, then dies with `subprocess.CalledProcessError: Command '['ffmpeg', '-f', 'rawvideo', ...]' returned non-zero exit status 234.` plus raw ffmpeg stderr ('Unable to choose an output format') -- leaked internals, no mention of the supported extensions (gif/png/apng/svg/mp4/mov/avi). (b) `save_path='<missing-dir>/a.gif'` raises bare `FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '<missing-dir>'` naming only the directory, with no 'create the directory or fix save_path' guidance (static save_path behaves the same via savefig). Suggest validating extension and parent-directory existence before the animation pipeline runs, mirroring the quality of the animate= errors.

hyp.plot(d, animate=True, duration=1, frame_rate=15, save_path='/tmp/anim_small.xyz')

findings.title: animate_MDS.py emits two sklearn FutureWarnings on every run (MDS n_init and init defaults changing)
findings.description: Running animate_MDS.py verbatim prints: 'FutureWarning: The default value of `n_init` will change from 4 to 1 in 1.9' and 'FutureWarning: The default value of `init` will change from 'random' to 'classical_mds' in 1.10' from sklearn/manifold/_mds.py. These leak into gallery output and every user's console for reduce='MDS', and when sklearn flips the defaults the example's rendered trajectory will silently change. hypertools' MDS wrapper should pin n_init/init explicitly (or the example should pass them via reduce params).
